name: bluewater-13-chatgpt-sent-your-customer-somewhere-else
lines: Nine o'clock at night. A garage door jams half open, with the car stuck inside.
The owner doesn't open Google. She just asks her phone. Who's the best garage door repair near me?
It answers in one breath. Three names.
The best garage door company in town is not one of them.
This is how you lose a customer you never knew existed.
Meet Tess. She's a made up example, but you know her.
Eleven years fixing garage doors. Four point nine stars. Three hundred reviews.
Her whole business runs on one thing. People tell people.
So when the phone got quieter this fall, she blamed the weather. Then the economy.
She never thought to blame a robot.
The new word of mouth.
Here's what changed while she was working.
A year ago, out of every hundred people looking for a local business, six asked an AI.
This year, forty five did.
They don't type three words and scroll anymore. They ask a full question, like they'd ask a neighbour.
And the answer isn't a page of ten links and a map.
It's three or four names. Then it stops talking.
One study looked at three hundred and fifty thousand business locations.
ChatGPT recommended about one in a hundred.
So the question isn't, am I on page one. There is no page one. There's a short answer, and you're in it, or you're not.
The lunch table.
Tess found out on a Thursday, at lunch.
Her newest tech is twenty two. He said, nobody my age googles a business. We just ask.
Tess laughed. Fine. Ask it who's the best at garage doors around here.
He typed it in, and read the answer out loud.
First name. A company across town.
Second name. A franchise.
Third name. A guy who opened fourteen months ago.
Nobody at the table said anything.
Eleven years. Three hundred reviews. And the machine had never heard of her.
Why him.
That night she opened the new guy's website, ready to hate it.
It was ugly. But every service had its own page.
Broken spring. Door off track. Opener won't close. Each one said what it is, which towns he covers, and what it costs, from.
Then she opened her own. A slideshow. Quality you can trust. A phone number.
A person can feel quality. A machine can only read.
In one study, more than half of what ChatGPT pulled for local searches came straight from business websites.
The rest came from mentions and directories. Places that repeat who you are.
Even her reviews couldn't help. Three hundred of them said, great service.
His said, fixed a snapped spring in Coquitlam in an hour.
One of those is a compliment. The other is an answer.
Give it something to say.
So here's what Tess did. Three moves, and none of them is a trick.
One. Say it plainly. A page for each job you do. What it is, where you go, how fast, and a price that starts with, from.
Two. Say it the same everywhere. Same name, same number, same hours, on every site that lists you.
When five places agree about you, a machine believes it.
Three. Ask for reviews that tell the story.
Don't ask for five stars, and don't hand them the words. Just ask, how did it go? Tell it your way.
A real story, in their own words, is something a robot can quote.
Now the honest part. Nobody can promise the machine will say your name.
Ask it the same thing twice, and most of the names change.
But there's one thing it does every single time.
It skips the business it can't read.
Nine o'clock at night. Another door jams. Another owner asks her phone.
This time, there's something written down about Tess.
You're already good. Now give the machine something to say.
